title: Why Can You Feel Wet With No Water?

fin.small: Sources: Filingeri et al., J Neurophysiol 112 (2014); Filingeri et al., J Appl Physiol 117 (2014)

parts: Your skin has no sensor for wet. Not one.
So how do you know your sock is wet? Stay for the dry test that fooled volunteers.
Researchers at Loughborough University say your brain works it out.
It mixes two signals: cold, and touch.
Volunteers touched equal drops of water at different temperatures.
Cold and wet felt the wettest. Warm and wet felt less wet.
Same water. But the strangest test used no water at all.
Just a dry probe, fifteen degrees Celsius colder than the skin.
Nothing wet touched them. Some volunteers still felt wet.
Dull the nerves for cold and touch, and the wet feeling fades.
Their model: wet is not something your skin measures. It is your brain's best guess.
So that damp feeling may just be a guess.
